posts.title: Show HN: gitclone-doctor, compare GitHub HTTPS access with HTTP/1.1
posts.first_comment:
I built gitclone-doctor to compare anonymous GitHub ref discovery with Git's selected HTTP transport and a forced HTTP/1.1 retry. It probes the target with the selected settings and HTTP/1.1, then repeats those two git ls-remote requests against the control. The control uses the target's frozen transport snapshot so a URL-specific proxy or CA choice does not silently change between sides.

The README GIF uses a local smart-HTTP fixture. Git itself makes the requests. The fixture returns 403 to the target over HTTP/2, serves refs over HTTP/1.1, and allows both control requests. It does not describe a current GitHub incident.

The probe clears Git helpers and extra headers, forces certificate verification, disables redirects, and stops if .netrc or _netrc exists. It checks ref discovery only, so it cannot confirm pack transfer, LFS, or submodules. I would value feedback on whether the comparison is useful and whether these limits are clear: https://github.com/Arthur031221/gitclone-doctor

posts.title: I built a CLI to compare GitHub ref discovery over HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1
posts.body:
I built gitclone-doctor to compare anonymous ref discovery for one public GitHub repository. It runs git ls-remote against the target with its selected transport settings and HTTP/1.1, then repeats those two requests against git/git. The control uses the same frozen proxy and CA snapshot.

The demo is a local smart-HTTP fixture, not a report of a current GitHub incident. Git makes the requests: the fixture returns HTTP 403 for the target over HTTP/2, returns refs over HTTP/1.1, and serves both control requests. The tool also keeps raw traces and config values out of its report.

This checks ref discovery only. It does not verify pack transfer, LFS, submodules, or authenticated access. I would appreciate feedback on whether the output explains what changed without implying why. Project: https://github.com/Arthur031221/gitclone-doctor

posts.body: I built gitclone-doctor to compare GitHub ref discovery with Git's selected HTTPS transport and an HTTP/1.1 retry. It reports observations, not a clone guarantee: https://github.com/Arthur031221/gitclone-doctor

I built gitclone-doctor as a small diagnostic for public GitHub HTTPS ref discovery. It compares the selected Git transport with HTTP/1.1 for both the requested repository and a control repository, using one frozen set of target transport settings.

The included GIF records actual Git requests to a controlled local smart-HTTP fixture. Its HTTP/2 error and HTTP/1.1 success are generated by that fixture and do not describe a current GitHub incident. The diagnostic is intentionally limited: a successful ls-remote does not establish that pack transfer, LFS, or submodules will work.

I would value feedback on whether the output separates useful observations from conclusions clearly. Source and local demo: https://github.com/Arthur031221/gitclone-doctor

posts.title: Comparing GitHub HTTPS ref discovery with HTTP/1.1
posts.body:
I built gitclone-doctor to compare Git's selected HTTPS transport with HTTP/1.1 for a public GitHub repository. It runs `git ls-remote URL HEAD` against the target with the selected settings and HTTP/1.1, then repeats those two requests against the `git/git` control repository. The control reuses the same frozen proxy and CA snapshot, so URL-specific transport settings do not quietly change between sides.

![Local smart-HTTP fixture showing an HTTP/2 403 and HTTP/1.1 ref discovery](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Arthur031221/gitclone-doctor/main/assets/demo.gif)

The GIF is a controlled local fixture, not a current GitHub incident. The fixture generates a temporary certificate, accepts HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1, and returns a deliberate 403 for the target over HTTP/2. It serves a valid smart-HTTP ref advertisement over HTTP/1.1. The control path succeeds over both protocols. The program checks its real Git trace and refuses to show the comparison if it cannot observe those requests.

The report contains response protocols and numeric statuses, not raw stderr, headers, config values, or trace text. Child Git processes use a rebuilt environment, clear helpers and extra headers, disable redirects, and require verified TLS. The tool refuses when `.netrc` or `_netrc` exists or cannot be checked, because Git's libcurl may consult those files. It does not read them.

The report also separates Git requests from direct network checks. Git uses the selected proxy when configured, while DNS and TLS checks bypass proxies and have their own deadlines. A direct DNS failure does not overturn passing Git requests. JSON contains fixed result codes and presence flags for helpers, headers, and URL rewrites, not the configured values.

This is a ref discovery check. It does not complete the clone pack transfer and does not test LFS, submodules, or authenticated access. A shared failure can remain unresolved, and an HTTP/1.1 success does not prove a protocol defect.

Run the local example with `npm run demo`. The CLI can be run from GitHub with `npx --yes --package=github:Arthur031221/gitclone-doctor gitclone-doctor git/git`. I would like feedback on whether the comparison is clear and whether its limits are stated plainly.

Repository: https://github.com/Arthur031221/gitclone-doctor
